Long ago, a young man named Giovanni Guasconti left his home in the south of Italy and came to Padua to pursue his studies at its ancient and famous university. <break time="0.8s" /> Having only a few coins in his pocket, he took a high and gloomy chamber in an old mansion, which had once belonged to a noble family of Padua. <break time="0.8s" /> Looking down from his window, Giovanni saw a garden of rare plants, in whose center stood the ruin of a marble fountain that still sent up its sparkling water. <break time="0.8s" /> A soft gurgling rose to his window and made him feel as if the fountain were an immortal spirit, singing its song endlessly without heeding the changes around it. <break time="0.8s" /> Beside the fountain grew a shrub with purple blossoms, each of which had the luster of a gem, and the whole was so bright that it seemed able to illuminate the garden even had there been no sunshine. <break time="0.8s" /> Soon a tall, thin, sallow man in a scholars black gown came into the garden and examined each plant with a cold, intent gaze, as though reading its innermost secrets. <break time="0.8s" /> Though his hands were gloved, he avoided even their scent, and when he reached the purple shrub, he placed a mask over his mouth, as if its beauty concealed a deadly malice. <break time="0.8s" /> He called for his daughter Beatrice, a girl as radiant as the blossoms themselves, who bent over the shrub without fear, embraced it, and whispered, Yes, my sister, your breath is the breath of life to me.

The next day Giovanni called on Professor Pietro Baglioni, an old friend of his father, who received him warmly and spoke with a cheerful ease that softened his learned dignity. <break time="0.8s" /> When Giovanni mentioned Rappaccini, the professor admitted that Rappaccini was as skillful as any doctor in Italy, but warned that he cared infinitely more for science than for mankind. <break time="0.8s" /> His patients interest him only as subjects for some new experiment, said Baglioni, and he would sacrifice human life, his own among the rest, to add a grain of mustard seed to his knowledge. <break time="0.8s" /> Baglioni, whose long rivalry with Rappaccini was well known, added that the daughter was rumored to be so learned that she might already fill a professors chair at the university. <break time="0.8s" /> That evening, from his window, Giovanni watched Beatrice pluck one of the purple flowers, and a drop of moisture from its broken stem fell upon a small lizard creeping at her feet. <break time="0.8s" /> The creature twisted for a moment and then lay motionless in the sunshine, and soon a bright insect, hovering near her face, drooped and fell lifeless at her feet, as if poisoned by her breath. <break time="0.8s" /> Hardly knowing what he did, Giovanni threw down a fresh bouquet he had bought that day, and Beatrice, smiling with a mixture of childish and womanly delight, picked it up. <break time="0.8s" /> As she turned back toward the house, Giovanni fancied that the flowers were already beginning to wither in her grasp, though at such a distance he could hardly be sure of it.
